Chapter 1 spoke as "we." Here the writer says "I" for the first time and calls the readers "my little children." Eleven of the letter's thirteen mentions of its own writing fall in this chapter. It tests claims by what is done, warns about the world and those who left, and ends at being "born from him."

The aim is spoken to "you": "so that you may not sin." The provision includes the writer: "we have an advocate." Beside "if anyone sins" the letter later sets "everyone who remains in him does not sin" (3:6) and "he cannot sin" (3:9). The Greek word for "atonement" is found in the New Testament only here and at 4:10. Read as "atonement," it speaks of sins made up for; as "appeasement," of anger turned away. Job 16:19-21. Job says his witness is "in the heavens" and weeps to God "that he would argue for a man with God." Verse 1: "we have an advocate with the Father." John 14:16. "Advocate" is found in the New Testament only in John 14-16, where it is the spirit (John 14:26), and in verse 1, where it is Jesus Christ.

Verses 4 and 5 are a pair: in the one who does not keep, "the truth is not in this person"; in the one who keeps, "truly in this person the love of God has been made complete." "The love of God" can mean his love or love for him. "Ought" comes three times in the letter, each tied to something already done: "just as that one walked" (verse 6), "that one laid down his life" (3:16), "God loved us" (4:11). Jeremiah 22:16. Yahweh calls judging the cause of the afflicted what it is "to know me." Verse 3 finds knowing him in keeping "his commandments."
The old commandment and the new

Verse 7 calls the commandment old, one they "had from the beginning." Verse 8 calls it new and gives a time: "the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining." Neither verse names it. The next three turn on a brother loved or hated, and 3:11 names what was heard from the beginning: "that we should love one another." In verse 11 the darkness is where he is, then where he walks, then what acts: it "has blinded his eyes." Read "in him" (verse 10), the one who loves holds no cause of stumbling; read "in it," the light holds none. Proverbs 4:18-19. Light growing to full day, and darkness where they "do not know what they stumble over": verses 8-11 have both. John 12:35. Verse 11 too "walks in the darkness," and in Greek "does not know where he is going" is the same in both, word for word.
To children, fathers and young men

Two rounds of three: children, fathers, young men. The fathers hear the same reason both times, word for word in Greek. The young men's second reason grows: they "are strong," and "the word of God remains" in them. Read "because," these are why he writes; read "that," what he writes. Elsewhere all the readers are "little children" (verses 1, 28) and "young children" (verse 18); the text does not say whether these groups are ages. Psalms 25:11. The psalm asks forgiveness "for the sake of your name"; its only other reason is that the guilt "is great." Verse 12: "on account of his name." John 16:33. Jesus says "I myself have conquered"; verses 13-14 tell the young men "you have conquered," the same verb in the same tense.

Verse 15 is the letter's first command; before it, verses 12-14 say only what is already true of the readers. "World" comes six times in three verses. It first came in verse 2, as how far the atonement reaches. It "is passing away," the verb used of the darkness in verse 8. Read "of possessions," verse 16 speaks of pride in what one owns (as at 3:17); read "of life," of pride in how one lives. Isaiah 40:8. Isaiah sets what fades against "the word of our God"; verse 17, the passing world against "the one who does the will of God," who "remains forever." John 3:16. God "loved the world." Verse 15 says, "Do not love the world." The Greek verb and noun are the same.

"From us" comes four times in verse 19, and their going out was "so that they might be revealed." Read "none of them are from us," this speaks of those who left; read "not all are from us," of the group: not everyone in it was from it. In this section the first "remain" is about those who did not: "they would have remained with us." From verse 19 to verse 28 it comes seven times. Read "all of you know" (verse 20), no one is left out; read "you know all things," compare "concerning all things" (verse 27). In verse 4 "a liar" does not keep the commandments; in verse 22 "the liar" denies "that Jesus is the Christ." The writer, teaching by letter, says they "have no need for anyone to teach" them (verse 27); in verse 21 he writes "because you know it." "Remain in him" (verse 27) can also be read as a statement. Jeremiah 31:34. No one will need to say "Know Yahweh," because all will know him. Verse 27: "no need for anyone to teach you"; verse 20: "all of you know." John 6:66-69. Many "went back." Peter says Jesus has "words of eternal life" and that they "have come to know" he is "the Holy One of God." Verses 19-25 also have leaving, "the Holy One," knowing and "the eternal life."

Verse 28 repeats "remain in him" from verse 27. The command is to "you"; the boldness and the shame are "we," the writer with them. The chapter began with "the righteous one" (verse 1) and ends with "he is righteous." Verses 28 and 29 do not name "him": the one who is coming, the one people are born from. John 3:8. The wind is heard, though no one knows where it comes from: "it is this way with everyone who has been born from the spirit." In verse 29 too the birth is known by what is done.
